items.prompt: What are carnassial teeth, and how do they help a predator eat meat?

options.label: A pair of blade-like teeth that slide past each other like scissors
options.feedback: Set at an angle, the upper and lower blade shear through muscle and hide in one stroke.

options.label: Flat teeth that grind meat into a paste
options.feedback: Grinding is what a herbivore's molars do to plant matter. Meat is sliced, not milled.

options.label: Hollow teeth that inject venom into prey
options.feedback: Venom delivery belongs to a small number of unrelated mammals, and none of them uses it through a shearing tooth.

options.label: Teeth that continue growing throughout life
options.feedback: That trait belongs to gnawing animals wearing their teeth down on hard food, not to a meat-eater's cutting teeth.

items.ok_line: Two blades passing each other, shearing through meat like a pair of scissors.
items.ko_line: Picture two teeth meeting edge to edge rather than crushing flat against each other.
items.exp_text: A carnassial is one upper and one lower tooth, each with a straight cutting edge, positioned so the two edges cross as the jaw closes rather than meeting flat. That crossing motion shears through muscle, tendon and hide the way a pair of scissors cuts cloth, far more efficiently than a flat bite could manage. Cats, dogs and many other meat-eating mammals carry this pair set back along the jaw, angled to catch the food as it is pulled sideways.

items.prompt: Why can a cat pull its claws back in, while a dog cannot?

options.label: A ligament in the cat's paw pulls the claw in by default
options.feedback: The claw rests sheathed unless a separate muscle actively extends it, the opposite of how a dog's paw is built.

options.label: A cat's claws are made of softer material
options.feedback: Claw material is the same in both animals. What differs is how the claw is anchored and moved, not what it is made of.

options.label: A cat has fewer toes than a dog
options.feedback: Both animals have a similar number of toes on each paw. Toe count has nothing to do with a claw sheathing.

options.label: A cat's claws stop growing earlier
options.feedback: Claws in both animals grow throughout life. Growth rate plays no part in whether a claw can be sheathed.

items.ok_line: Resting sheathed, and pulled out only when a muscle calls for it.
items.ko_line: Look at what the claw is doing when the paw is simply resting, not when it is in use.
items.exp_title: Sheathed by default, drawn by choice
items.exp_text: In a cat's paw, a ligament holds each claw pulled back into a sheath of skin whenever the toe muscles are relaxed, keeping the tip off the ground and out of the way as the cat walks. A separate muscle has to contract to draw the claw forward and expose it, which the cat does deliberately when climbing, gripping or striking. A dog's paw has no such ligament: its claws sit permanently extended, which is why they click on a hard floor with every step.

items.prompt: What lets a cheetah's stride lengthen so much while it is sprinting after prey?

options.label: Its spine flexes and stretches with every stride
options.feedback: Bending and straightening, the spine adds extra reach to each stride beyond what the legs alone provide.

options.label: Its legs are jointed in an extra place
options.feedback: A cheetah's leg bones and joints are arranged much like those of any other cat. Nothing extra has been added there.

options.label: Its tail pushes it forward like a paddle
options.feedback: The tail acts as a counterbalance for sudden turns. It never touches the ground, so it cannot push against anything.

options.label: Its front paws grip the ground with suction
options.feedback: Nothing about a paw can create suction on open ground. Grip here comes from claws digging in, not from any seal.

items.ok_line: A spine that curls and uncurls, adding reach that the legs alone could never give.
items.ko_line: The extra reach in the stride is coming from the middle of the body, not from the legs or paws.
items.exp_title: A spine that works like a spring
items.exp_text: As a cheetah gathers its legs beneath it mid-stride, its spine curls tightly, and as the legs then push apart again the spine snaps back straight, throwing the front and back legs further apart than their own length would allow. This flexing adds a burst of extra reach to every stride on top of what the legs themselves provide, so the whole body works as one long spring rather than four separate limbs. Non-retractable claws dig in like cleats to keep that spring from slipping.

items.prompt: Why do wolves hunt large prey together rather than alone?

options.label: Together they can tire and corner an animal too strong for one wolf
options.feedback: Taking turns to chase, they wear an animal down and box it in from several sides at once, something a lone wolf cannot manage.

options.label: A pack confuses prey with its scent alone
options.feedback: Scent may alert prey to danger, but it does nothing on its own to bring an animal down once the chase begins.

options.label: Hunting together lets each wolf hunt less often
options.feedback: A pack still has to hunt whenever it is hungry. Cooperation changes how prey is caught, not how often eating is needed.

options.label: It keeps the pack's territory from shrinking
options.feedback: Marking and defending territory is a separate behaviour from the hunt itself, and does not explain why several wolves chase one animal together.

items.ok_line: Numbers succeed against prey that strength alone could not bring down.
items.ko_line: Think about what a moose or a bison can do to a single attacker, and what changes when several attack from different sides.
items.exp_title: Strength in numbers against a stronger animal
items.exp_text: An elk or a bison can kill a wolf with a single kick, so a lone wolf attacking one head-on risks its life for little chance of success. A pack instead splits up, some wolves chasing to exhaust the animal while others cut off its escape, and they take turns biting so no single wolf bears the full risk of the prey's horns or hooves. By sharing both the chase and the danger, the pack brings down an animal none of them could handle by itself.

items.prompt: How does a big cat typically finish off large prey once it has caught it?

options.label: With a bite that clamps the throat until the prey suffocates
options.feedback: Locking its jaws around the windpipe, the cat cuts off the animal's air rather than tearing it open.

options.label: By striking repeatedly with its front paws
options.feedback: The paws help pin the prey down. The kill itself comes from the jaws, not from repeated blows.

options.label: By exhausting the prey until it collapses from fatigue
options.feedback: That describes how pack hunters like wolves often work, wearing an animal down over a chase. A big cat generally kills in one sudden bite instead.

options.label: By waiting for the prey to bleed out slowly
options.feedback: A slow bleed would let injured prey escape or fight back. Cats instead aim for a hold that ends the struggle quickly.

items.ok_line: A grip on the throat, held until the prey has no air left to fight with.
items.ko_line: Think about where on the body the cat's jaws close, and what stopping that part of the body achieves.
items.exp_text: Once a big cat has pulled large prey down, it typically clamps its jaws around the animal's throat and holds on rather than biting repeatedly, using its whole body weight to keep the grip in place. This seals off the windpipe, and the prey loses consciousness from lack of air within a couple of minutes. The same throat hold works whether the cat is a lion pulling down a buffalo or a jaguar surprising prey from an ambush.

items.prompt: Why is a lion's tongue rough enough to feel like sandpaper?

options.label: Backward-curving spines on it rasp meat and fur from bone
options.feedback: Each tiny hook catches and pulls, working like a row of small combs dragged across the carcass.

options.label: It helps the lion taste blood more strongly
options.feedback: Taste buds are separate from these spines, and roughness does not sharpen a sense of taste.

options.label: It grips slippery prey during the chase
options.feedback: The tongue stays inside the mouth during a chase. It plays no part in gripping prey that is still running.

options.label: It cools the lion down by trapping air
options.feedback: Panting cools a lion by evaporating moisture from a wet tongue. Trapping air is not part of how that works.

items.ok_line: Hundreds of tiny backward hooks, dragging meat off the bone.
items.ko_line: Feel for what the roughness actually does once the lion starts eating, rather than before.
items.exp_title: A tongue covered in tiny hooks
items.exp_text: A lion's tongue is covered in small, backward-pointing spines made of the same hard material as claws, called papillae, and each one catches on meat or fur as the tongue drags across it. Pulled toward the throat, hundreds of these hooks together strip flesh cleanly from bone and comb loose fur out of a lion's own coat when it grooms. The same rasping action that helps at a carcass is what a house cat's smaller version does to your skin if it licks you.

items.prompt: Why do many predator cats, like leopards and tigers, have spotted or striped coats?

options.label: The pattern breaks up their outline against the background
options.feedback: Scattered patches confuse the eye about where the animal's edge actually is, hiding its shape rather than its colour.

options.label: It signals rank to other members of the same species
options.feedback: Coat pattern stays fixed for life and does not change with status. Signalling rank calls for something that can vary.

options.label: It helps the cat stay cool in hot climates
options.feedback: Pattern has no effect on how much heat a coat lets through. Colour and thickness matter for that, not the shape of the markings.

options.label: It makes the cat easier for its cubs to spot
options.feedback: A pattern built to stand out would also catch the eye of the prey the cat is trying to approach unseen.

items.ok_line: Not a colour trick but a shape trick, breaking the outline apart.
items.ko_line: The pattern matters most in a very particular moment: while the cat is trying not to be seen at all.
items.exp_title: Hiding the outline, not the colour
items.exp_text: A solid block of colour, even a good match to the background, still shows up as one continuous shape once an eye looks for it. Spots and stripes instead break that shape into pieces that blend into the dappled light of grass or forest, so the cat's edges dissolve into the surroundings rather than matching a single background colour. A tiger's stripes work especially well among vertical reeds and stems, exactly the setting it hunts in, letting it close the distance on prey before being noticed.

items.prompt: How does a wolf's nose let it track prey it cannot yet see?

options.label: Moist tissue inside the nose captures scent molecules from the air
options.feedback: Wet surfaces trap and dissolve odour molecules efficiently, holding them still long enough for scent receptors to detect them.

options.label: It hears the prey's footsteps through the ground
options.feedback: Detecting vibration through the ground is a different sense entirely, and it is not something a nose does.

options.label: It feels changes in air pressure ahead
options.feedback: Air pressure shifts are far too small and slow to reveal where a moving animal has gone.

options.label: It senses body heat given off by the prey
options.feedback: Detecting heat at a distance calls for a different kind of organ, one no wolf possesses. A nose responds to chemicals, not warmth.

items.ok_line: A wet surface that catches scent out of the air and holds it there to be read.
items.ko_line: The nose is always damp for a reason. That dampness is doing the actual work of catching a scent.
items.exp_title: A damp surface built to catch a scent
items.exp_text: The skin around a wolf's nostrils is kept moist, and that moisture dissolves scent molecules drifting past, holding them against the tissue instead of letting them float on. Air pulled in then carries those trapped molecules over a folded surface packed with scent receptors, far more of them than a human nose has, letting the wolf pick apart individual scents layered on top of each other. A trail left by prey hours earlier can still be read this way, molecule by faint molecule.

items.prompt: What lets a hyena's jaw crack open bones that most predators leave behind?

options.label: A wide skull anchoring unusually large jaw muscles
options.feedback: More muscle bulk, attached across a broader area of bone, delivers far more crushing force per bite.

options.label: Teeth made of a harder mineral than other predators'
options.feedback: Tooth mineral is essentially the same across mammal predators. The difference lies in force, not in what the teeth are made of.

options.label: A jaw that can open far wider than usual
options.feedback: Cracking a bone needs crushing force, not extra reach. A wider gape alone would not add any strength to the bite.

options.label: Venom that softens bone before biting
options.feedback: No predator produces a substance that softens bone. The bone is broken by force alone, applied directly.

items.ok_line: A broad skull built to anchor unusually powerful muscle.
items.ko_line: Cracking bone takes raw crushing force. Think about where that force comes from.
items.exp_title: A skull built around its muscles
items.exp_text: A hyena's skull is unusually wide and heavily built compared with its body size, and that width gives its jaw muscles a broad surface to attach to and a long lever to pull against. The bigger and better anchored those muscles are, the more force the jaw can deliver at the back teeth, where the crushing actually happens. That extra force is what lets a hyena do something few other predators manage, splitting open a bone to reach the marrow inside rather than leaving it for scavengers.

items.prompt: Why does a polar bear's coat look white, even though the skin underneath it is black?

options.label: Its hairs are colourless and hollow, scattering light so it looks white
options.feedback: Each hair is a clear, hollow tube; light bounces around inside and scatters back out looking white, while some of it still reaches the dark skin beneath.

options.label: Its skin releases a white pigment onto the hair
options.feedback: Pigment builds colour into hair as it grows from the root, and it would not turn the skin black while doing so.

options.label: The cold air bleaches the hair over time
options.feedback: Cold has no bleaching effect on hair. Colour here comes from the hair's structure, not from weathering.

options.label: Ice crystals coat every hair permanently
options.feedback: A bear's coat looks white long before any ice forms on it, in warm weather included, so ice cannot be the explanation.

items.ok_line: Clear, hollow hairs scattering light, with dark skin waiting underneath.
items.ko_line: Look at what each individual hair is made of and shaped like, rather than at the coat as a whole.
items.exp_text: Each hair in a polar bear's coat has no pigment at all and is hollow down its length, so light entering it bounces around inside and scatters back out in every direction, which the eye reads as white. That same hollow structure also lets some light pass all the way through to the skin beneath, and the skin is black, which absorbs that light efficiently and turns it into warmth. The coat that looks like snow is quietly funnelling sunlight down to a surface built to soak it up.
